blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A table arranges data in rows and columns under clear headings, so that it can be read and compared without any graphical element. A frequency distribution (recall §1.4.1) is one kind of table; a cross-tabulation (two-way table) is another, showing how two categorical variables are distributed jointly.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A well-labelled grid is already a large gain in readability over a raw list. Tables also do something charts cannot: they keep exact values. A chart trades exactness for visual impact.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A table listing several districts down the rows and their CBHI membership percentages across the columns lets you compare exact figures. A chart of the same numbers would let you judge them only by eye.

points.html: A good table has a title that says what, where and when; labelled rows and columns with units; totals where they help; and a footnote naming the data source. Give all four in every thesis or manuscript table.
Use a table when exact values matter (for example, when a reviewer must check your figures); use a chart when the shape or trend matters more than the exact numbers.
The cross-tabulation is the starting point for the chi-square test of independence (§10.6.1, a test of whether two categorical variables are associated).
